messages.mes:
The road took him down from the verge between plowed fields, and the walls grew as he walked — grey stone, older than anything he'd seen on Earth, patched in places with newer, paler masonry. The traffic thickened: carts of turnips, a drover prodding geese with a switch, two women in muddy aprons walking fast and talking about someone named Hessa. A cartwheel creaked somewhere behind him the whole way.

At the gate, a bored guard in a quilted jerkin glanced at the staff in Alaric's hand, then at his face, and waved him through without a word. A coin-box stood to one side with a sign saying tolls applied to carts and beasts only.

Inside, the noise hit first — hammering from a smithy off the main street, a boy crying fish, shutters clattering open. Morning light came down narrow between timber-framed buildings, and the smell was bread, straw, and horse. People brushed past him without a second look.

He asked nothing and found it anyway: a wide, two-storey building of dark timber with a carved sign hanging above the door — a sword crossed with an arrow, paint faded but legible. A pair of muddy boots on the step told him what kind of people came and went.

The door swung open on a large hall that smelled of lamp oil and spilled ale, though the morning had barely begun. A long notice board ran along the left wall, papered with contract slips. To the right, a heavy oak counter with a young clerk behind it, red-haired, freckled, copying something into a ledger. Down the middle of the room, three long tables; two of them held dozing men with swords propped against benches and half-drunk cups of something that steamed.

A dog lifted its head from under one table and looked at him.

The clerk looked up too, pen pausing.

"Morning. Help you, or are you here to read the board?"

messages.mes:
"Alaric Red." The clerk set the pen down in the ledger's groove and pulled a fresh sheet toward herself. "Maren. Welcome to the Alderwatch branch."

She reached under the counter and produced a slate-backed tablet, thin as a plank, its surface dark and faintly glossy. Her palm flattened on it for a moment and the surface shimmered.

"Registration's simple. Name, age — you look of age, so I'll not ask for proof — and a reading off the stone." She nodded toward a squat pillar of grey crystal standing at the counter's end, worn smooth where thousands of hands had rested. "You touch it, it tells us your Power Rank. That's your strength — F through S — and the Guild can't give it to you or take it away. What we do grant is Guild Rank. You'd start at Novice, and you climb by doing contracts, not by killing anything impressive in an alley."

She turned the tablet around and slid a small brass dish across the counter beside it.

"Fee is two silver, once, and it's yours for life — any branch in any kingdom honors the mark. Pays for the record, the slip enchantment, the medallion." She tapped the dish. "Coin first, then the stone, then I write you in."

Behind him, one of the dozing men coughed and pulled his cup closer without waking.

"Questions before you pay, or shall we go on?"

She pressed a small metal plate into his hands — palm-sized, dull pewter, the Guild's crossed sword-and-arrow stamped into it, his name etched beneath in thin, careful lines. The metal warmed faintly against his skin, alive in some small way.

messages.mes:
Alaric laid the slip on the counter. Maren read it, stamped the Guild's seal into the ledger column beside his name, and dipped the pen once more.

"Skeletons in the Upper Burial Galleries. Active as of now." She blew across the wet ink, then held out the slip — the paper carried a faint warmth, like a sun-warmed windowsill, the same enchantment that tied it to the rolls. "Keep that on you. It's your word the work is yours."

She pulled a thin folder from a drawer and slid out a smaller sheet, handing it over with the slip.

"The chapel's an hour west by the west road — you'll see it from the road before you reach it, broken tower, yew trees. The temple wardens keep a lodge there; they're the ones who posted the work, so they'll know what you've come for when you walk in. The upper galleries are the first level, under the chapel floor. They can tell you which stair to take." She closed the folder. "When the work's done, you come back here — or any Guild desk anywhere — and turn the slip in with whatever shows it's done. That's when you get paid. Not before, and not from the wardens' own hands. The Guild pays its own."

She straightened the slip's corner where it had curled.

"Sixty copper on turn-in. Any questions, I'm here most days. Otherwise — the road's that way." A nod toward the doors.

messages.mes:
The west road carried him out of Alderwatch between morning carts and a flock of geese driven by a boy with a willow switch, and then the city was behind him and the country opened — hedgerows, turnip fields, a wind that smelled of wet earth and woodsmoke. The road ran gently uphill. Carts overtook him, none of them interested in him; a woman walking the other way with a basket of eggs nodded without slowing.

A little past the hour, the chapel showed itself exactly as Maren had said: a broken tower rising over a stand of yews, dark and heavy against the pale sky, the nave's roof fallen in on one side so the rafters stuck up like ribs. A low wall circled the grounds, and a wooden lodge stood inside it near the gate, smoke rising thin from its chimney.

The yard told the rest. Graves in rows, old stones weathered smooth, and a stretch of freshly turned ground at the far end — two or three plots dug and then left open, empty, grass beginning to dry in the upturned soil. Work stopped mid-job and never picked up again.

Near the chapel's flank, a man in a grey habit was stacking firewood against the lodge wall. Older, broad through the shoulders, sleeves rolled despite the chill. He heard the gate hinge and looked up, taking Alaric in — the staff, the robes, the Guild slip's corner showing where it was tucked.

"You'll be from the Guild, then." He set the last billet on the stack and straightened, working a kink out of his back. "We've had the notice two days. Didn't think they'd send someone so quick." He wiped his hands on his thighs and nodded toward the chapel door, where a board lay nailed across a lower doorway like a lid on a box. From somewhere beneath the ground, faint through the morning quiet, came a sound like dry bone shifting on stone.

messages.mes:
The road took him back the way he had come, and the warden walked with him as far as the chapel door, pulling the board off the lower doorway with a grunt and leaning it against the stone.

"Stair's straight down. Galleries run in a loop — old burial corridors, alcoves on both sides. They don't wander far from their bones." He stepped back and picked up his axe from the woodpile. "I'll be at the lodge."

The stair was narrow, worn hollow in the middle by centuries of feet, and cold rose up it like water. Torch brackets lined the wall, empty. Alaric's staff gave off a faint arc-light glow — enough to see by — and the light slid over stone, over bones set into the walls themselves in niches stacked to the ceiling, skulls facing inward.

The sound from below grew clearer as he descended: a dry clicking, a slow drag, pause, drag. At the bottom the stair opened into a long corridor of pale stone, the arc-light reaching perhaps twenty paces down it. Alcoves opened off both sides, some sealed with slabs, some gaping.

Twenty paces ahead, something stood against the wall in one of the alcoves. It had the shape of a man and none of the flesh — yellowed bone, a skull tipped at an angle of long disuse, one arm hanging with a rusted knife still gripped in the finger bones. As the light touched it, the skull turned. The jaw worked once, soundlessly. Then it stepped out of the alcove, unhurried, bones scraping, and started toward him down the corridor.

messages.mes:
He went down. The gallery ran straight at first, then bent left past a slab where a coffin lid had been shoved aside and its occupant long since spilled to bare bone. Alaric gave that one a wide berth and kept the staff up as he walked, boots scuffing on grit, the wound at his flank pulling with each stride.

The alcoves thinned. The walls changed from stacked niches to plain fitted stone, older and darker, and the air came colder from ahead, moving faintly against his face — a draft, which meant another opening somewhere. His light reached the bend in the corridor and no farther.

There he stopped at the edge of it, and the corridor opened into a low chamber.

Three stone biers stood in a row down its middle, each with a body laid out on top — or what was left of bodies, cloth rotted to rags over bone. One bier was empty, its lid cracked on the floor beside it. A second doorway gaped in the far wall, a black mouth with steps leading down, and the draft breathed out of it with a smell that sat wrong in the nose: old meat, damp, something sour underneath.

Scratches marked the floor between the biers. Long furrows in the stone dust, as if something had been dragged, and the marks ran into the far doorway and down.

He stood at the bend with the light on the chamber, blood drying stiff at his hip, mana still shallow in him. Nothing in the room moved. The empty bier said something had; the stairs said where it had gone.

messages.mes:
The stairs were narrow and worn hollow in the middle, each step dished by feet centuries dead. Alaric went down with the staff first, light swinging, and the sour smell thickened as he descended — old meat and damp, pressed close in the stonework. His boots echoed wrong down the shaft, too loud, and he slowed his pace without deciding to.

Forty steps, maybe fifty. The stairway ended in another corridor, and this one was different from the galleries above. No alcoves here. The walls were black stone, slick in places with a thin wet sheen his light caught and lost, and the ceiling lowered until the staff's top nearly brushed it. Bones lay scattered along the floor's edges — not arranged, not stacked. Strewn. A rib cage here, a jaw there, a scatter of small hand bones as if something had been eaten and the leavings kicked aside.

The drag furrows continued. In the stone dust of this corridor they were deeper, fresher-edged, and they did not wander — they ran a straight line down the passage's center, ahead into the dark where his light failed.

And under the sour smell, faint but unmistakable, came a sound: a wet, rhythmic noise, far down the corridor. Something working at something. It paused.

Then resumed.

The corridor offered one direction only — down that black throat, toward the sound — and the stairs back up stood at his rear. His mana sat full behind his ribs; the ache at his flank was only an ache. Whatever had dragged itself down here was within a hundred paces, and it had heard him.

messages.mes:
The wet sound carried farther as he eased down the corridor, step by careful step. Twenty paces. Thirty. He kept to the wall where the bone scatter thinned, setting each boot down flat, and the staff's light slid along the black stone ahead of him.

The leavings thickened. A splintered femur. A skull cracked open at the back. Small bones ground to chips, and the drag furrows widened here, with something dark dried in a long smear down the floor's center.

The stink hung thick enough to taste. Ahead, the corridor widened into a shallow hollow where the ceiling sagged, and the sound came from inside it.

He stopped at the lip of the opening.

The thing crouched with its back to him over what had been dragged down — a rotted corpse off one of the biers, cloth hanging in wet ribbons. It was man-shaped and wrong: gaunt past any living thinness, grey skin stretched over knobbled joints, arms too long, its spine ridged up under the skin from the hunch of it. Its head worked at the carcass, tearing, the sound of it loud in the cold.

Then it stopped.

The head turned over its shoulder, the body still crouched — a face with sunken cheeks, eyes that caught his light and held it, flat and bright. Gristle hung from its fingers. Its mouth opened, and what came out was a wet clicking, jaw working as if remembering how.

It rose off its haunches, unfolding taller than a man ought to fold, and its weight came forward onto the balls of its feet.
